title: Files & the os Package
summary: Read and write files with the **os** package. For whole small files use `os.ReadFile` / `os.WriteFile`; for streaming use `os.Open` / `os.Create` to get an `*os.File` and wrap it in a **bufio.Scanner** (read lines) or **bufio.Writer** (buffered writes). Always `defer f.Close()`, check errors, and flush buffered writers.

subtopics.title: Whole-file read & write
subtopics.explanation: os.ReadFile returns the entire file as a []byte in one call; os.WriteFile writes a []byte, creating or truncating the file with the given permission bits. They're the simplest option and perfect for small config files — but they load everything into memory, so avoid them for large files.

subtopics.title: Opening files: Open, Create, OpenFile
subtopics.explanation: os.Open opens a file read-only; os.Create makes (or truncates) a file for writing; os.OpenFile takes explicit flags (O_APPEND, O_CREATE, …) and a permission mode for full control. Each returns an *os.File, which you must Close — always with defer, right after checking the error.

subtopics.title: Reading line by line with bufio.Scanner
subtopics.explanation: For large files, stream them: wrap the *os.File in bufio.NewScanner and loop while Scan() returns true, reading each line with Text() (the newline is stripped). After the loop, check Err() — Scan() returns false for both end-of-file and errors, so the error check is how you tell them apart.

subtopics.title: Buffered writing & flushing
subtopics.explanation: Writing to a file one small piece at a time is slow. bufio.NewWriter batches writes in memory and sends them in larger chunks — but the buffer must be flushed. Call w.Flush() (commonly deferred) before the file closes, or the last buffered bytes never reach disk.

subtopics.title: Handling 'not found' and other errors
subtopics.explanation: File operations return errors you must handle. To detect a missing file specifically, test with errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist) (or os.IsNotExist(err)). Use filepath.Join to build paths so they work across operating systems rather than hardcoding '/'.

foundations.overview: The os package exposes the filesystem: convenience calls (ReadFile/WriteFile) for whole small files, and openers (Open/Create/OpenFile) that return an *os.File for streaming. Streaming reads pair the file with a bufio.Scanner (line-oriented) and streaming writes with a bufio.Writer (batched, must Flush). The consistent discipline is: check every error, defer Close immediately after opening, and for buffered writers, flush before close.
foundations.formalDefinition: os provides a platform-independent interface to operating-system functionality including file I/O. os.Open/Create/OpenFile return *os.File (implementing io.Reader/io.Writer/io.Closer); os.ReadFile/WriteFile handle a whole file in one call. Permissions use os.FileMode (e.g. 0o644).
foundations.whyItMatters: Services read config, write logs and exports, and process data files. Choosing whole-file vs streaming correctly controls memory use, and the close/flush/error discipline is what separates code that silently loses data from code that's reliable.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture two doors. The small door (ReadFile/WriteFile) hands you the whole file at once — easy, but the file must fit in memory. The big door (Open + bufio) gives you a stream you pull through a line at a time — a bit more code, but it handles files of any size with constant memory.
commonUseCases: Reading a small config or JSON file with os.ReadFile
Streaming a large log/CSV line by line with bufio.Scanner
Appending to a file with os.OpenFile + O_APPEND
Writing generated output efficiently with a buffered writer

commonMisconceptions.myth: os.ReadFile is fine for any file.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It loads the entire file into memory; for large files stream with os.Open + bufio.Scanner to keep memory constant.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Closing the *os.File flushes a bufio.Writer for you.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The buffer is in the bufio.Writer, not the file. If you don't call Flush, the last buffered bytes are lost even though the file closes cleanly.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If Scan() stops, the whole file was read.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Scan() returns false on both EOF and error (e.g. a line longer than the 64KB default). Always check scanner.Err() to distinguish them.

visualExplorer.title: The streaming read pipeline
visualExplorer.caption: Open the file, wrap it in a Scanner, pull lines until Scan() is false, then check Err and let defer Close run.

config.intro: Reading a large log file line by line without loading it all into memory:

steps.name: Open (check the error)
steps.detail: os.Open returns an *os.File and an error; if err != nil you return early and never touch the file.

steps.name: defer Close immediately
steps.detail: Right after the error check, defer f.Close() so the descriptor is released on every return path.

steps.name: Wrap in a Scanner
steps.detail: bufio.NewScanner(f) reads in chunks and hands you one line at a time — constant memory regardless of file size.

steps.name: Loop while Scan()
steps.detail: for sc.Scan() { use sc.Text() } processes each line; Text() has the trailing newline stripped.

steps.name: Check Err() after the loop
steps.detail: Scan() returned false — was it clean EOF or a read error / too-long line? sc.Err() tells you; nil means the whole file was read.

interactiveExamples.title: Write then read a whole file
interactiveExamples.explanation: os.WriteFile creates/truncates and writes bytes; os.ReadFile reads them all back. Convert between string and []byte as needed.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: fix the lost-write bug
interactiveExamples.explanation: This program writes through a bufio.Writer but the file ends up empty. Add the missing flush so the buffered bytes reach the file before it closes.

checkpoints.prompt: You must process a 5 GB log file on a machine with 1 GB RAM. Which approach?
options: os.Open + bufio.Scanner, looping line by line
Load it into a string and range over it
checkpoints.explanation: os.Open + bufio.Scanner streams the file with constant memory. The other options load the whole 5 GB into memory and will exhaust RAM.

checkpoints.prompt: out.txt is empty even though the program 'wrote' to it. Why?
checkpoints.code:
f, _ := os.Create("out.txt")
w := bufio.NewWriter(f)
fmt.Fprintln(w, "hello")
f.Close() // no Flush
options: The bufio.Writer's buffer was never flushed, so the bytes never reached the file
checkpoints.explanation: The data sits in the bufio.Writer's in-memory buffer. Closing the *os.File does not flush the writer, so the buffered bytes are lost. Call w.Flush() (or defer it) before Close.

checkpoints.prompt:
Given a file containing 'a

b
', what prints?
checkpoints.code:
sc := bufio.NewScanner(f)
n := 0
for sc.Scan() { n++ }
fmt.Println(n)
checkpoints.explanation: Scanner splits on newlines: 'a', '' (the blank line), and 'b' are three tokens, so n == 3. The trailing newline ends the last line rather than creating an extra empty one.

checkpoints.prompt: Detect specifically that a file is missing.
checkpoints.explanation: errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist) reports whether err is (or wraps) the sentinel for a missing file. errors.As is for extracting a concrete error type; New/Unwrap don't test identity.

codeLab.title: Count non-blank lines in a file
codeLab.instructions: Implement `CountNonBlank(path string) (int, error)` that opens the file, streams it with bufio.Scanner, and returns how many lines are not empty/whitespace-only. Return any open or scan error. Close the file with defer.
hints: os.Open returns an error you should return immediately if non-nil.
Return sc.Err() at the end so a read error propagates (it's nil on clean EOF).

debuggingLab.title: Program crashes with 'too many open files'
debuggingLab.symptom: A function that opens many files in a loop eventually fails with 'too many open files'.

brokenCode.expectedOutput: works for a while, then: too many open files

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Each os.Open consumes a file descriptor, a limited OS resource. Without Close, descriptors accumulate until the process hits its limit and further opens fail. defer inside the loop body would still hold them until the function returns, so close within the iteration.
commonMistakes: Using defer f.Close() at function scope inside a long loop, holding every descriptor until the end.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Close each file within the loop iteration (e.g. a helper with its own defer) so descriptors are released promptly.

solution.expectedOutput: processes all files without leaking descriptors

theory.question: When should you use os.ReadFile versus os.Open with a bufio.Scanner?
theory.directAnswer: Use os.ReadFile when the file is small and you want its whole contents as a []byte in one call — config files, small fixtures. Use os.Open plus bufio.Scanner when the file is large or unbounded, so you stream it line by line with constant memory instead of loading the entire thing into RAM.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two file-reading strategies: whole-file convenience versus streaming.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Small files are simplest read at once; large files must be streamed to bound memory.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: ReadFile allocates a []byte the size of the file; a Scanner reads fixed-size chunks and yields tokens (lines) without holding the whole file.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing wrong causes either needless complexity or out-of-memory failures on big inputs — a common practical decision.
theory.realWorldExample: Read a 2 KB YAML config with os.ReadFile; process a multi-gigabyte access log with os.Open + bufio.Scanner.

followUps.question: What's the risk of os.ReadFile on user-supplied files?
followUps.answer: A huge or malicious file can exhaust memory; stream it, or cap the size with an io.LimitReader.

theory.question: Why must you call Flush on a bufio.Writer, and where should Close and Flush go?
theory.directAnswer: A bufio.Writer buffers writes in memory and only sends them to the underlying file in chunks; the tail of the data stays buffered until you Flush. Closing the *os.File does not flush the writer, so without Flush the last bytes are lost. The idiom is: open/create, check err, defer f.Close(), create the writer, defer w.Flush() — and because defers run last-in-first-out, Flush runs before Close.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The buffering contract between bufio.Writer and the file beneath it.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Buffering batches small writes into fewer, larger syscalls for performance.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Flush drains the in-memory buffer to the file; deferring it (declared after the Close defer) guarantees it runs first on return.

theory.whyImportant: Silent data loss from a missing Flush is a classic, hard-to-spot bug, and the defer ordering is a frequent interview detail.
theory.realWorldExample: A report exporter buffered rows with bufio.Writer; adding defer w.Flush() fixed truncated output files.

followUps.question: For a buffered writer, should you also check the error from Flush/Close?
followUps.answer: Yes — on writes the final Flush (and Close) can surface disk-full or I/O errors that earlier buffered Writes hid; ignore them and you can lose data silently.

scenario.question: A batch job reading many files crashes with 'too many open files' after running a while. What's the likely cause and fix in Go?
scenario.directAnswer: It's a file-descriptor leak: files are opened in a loop but not closed, so descriptors accumulate until the process hits its ulimit. The fix is to close each file promptly — typically by moving the open/use/close into a helper function (or an inline closure) so defer f.Close() fires at the end of each iteration rather than at the end of the whole loop.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Descriptors are a bounded OS resource; a defer at function scope inside a big loop holds them all until return.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Wrapping each iteration's work in a function gives Close its own scope, releasing the descriptor immediately after processing that file.

scenario.whyImportant: It's a real production failure mode that only appears under volume, so understanding descriptor lifetime matters.
scenario.realWorldExample: An importer processing 100k files leaked descriptors until each file's handling was wrapped in a closure with its own defer Close.

followUps.question: How would you confirm it's a descriptor leak?
followUps.answer: Watch open descriptors (lsof / /proc/<pid>/fd) grow over time, and note the error is specifically 'too many open files' (EMFILE).

systemDesign.question: Design a memory-safe pipeline in Go that reads a huge CSV, transforms each row, and writes results to a new file.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Stream both ends. Open the input with os.Open and read rows with encoding/csv's Reader (which reads incrementally); open the output with os.Create wrapped in a bufio.Writer (and a csv.Writer). Process one row at a time in a loop — read, transform, write — so memory stays constant regardless of file size. defer Close on both files, defer the writer Flush, and check the final Flush/Close errors so a disk-full failure isn't swallowed. For throughput, optionally fan rows out to a bounded worker pool, preserving order if required.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A constant-memory read-transform-write pipeline over large files.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Loading a huge CSV fully into memory doesn't scale; streaming does.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: csv.Reader pulls records incrementally from the *os.File; each transformed record is written through a buffered csv.Writer; deferred Flush/Close finalize the output and surface errors.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It combines streaming I/O, the flush/close discipline, and error propagation — exactly the reliability concerns of real ETL code.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A nightly job rewrites a 10 GB export, normalizing a column, using csv.Reader/Writer over buffered files with steady memory.

followUps.question: Where would concurrency help, and what's the catch?
followUps.answer: CPU-heavy per-row transforms can go to a worker pool, but you must re-order results (or accept unordered output) and bound the pool to avoid unbounded memory.

followUps.question: How do you make the write atomic so a crash doesn't leave a half-written file?
followUps.answer: Write to a temp file in the same directory, Flush/Close/Sync it, then os.Rename it over the target — rename is atomic on the same filesystem.

coding.question: Implement `func Head(path string, n int) ([]string, error)` that returns the first n lines of a file (or all of them if the file is shorter), streaming so it never reads more than needed.
coding.thoughtProcess: Open the file and defer Close. Use a bufio.Scanner and loop, appending Text() to a slice; break as soon as I have n lines so I don't read the rest of a large file. After the loop, return the slice and scanner.Err(). Guard n <= 0 by returning an empty slice.
coding.lineByLine: We short-circuit n <= 0 to an empty slice. os.Open gives the file (returning its error), and defer f.Close() releases it on every path. A bufio.Scanner streams lines; we append each Text() and break the moment we've collected n, so a huge file isn't fully read. Finally we return the collected lines plus sc.Err(), which is nil on a clean read and non-nil if scanning failed.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) lines read (not the whole file).

followUps.question: Why break early instead of reading the whole file then slicing?
followUps.answer: Breaking avoids reading gigabytes when you only need the first few lines — the whole point of streaming with a Scanner.

followUps.question: What if a line exceeds the Scanner's default 64KB limit?
followUps.answer: Scan returns false and sc.Err() reports bufio.ErrTooLong; raise the limit with sc.Buffer(buf, max) or read with bufio.Reader.ReadString('\n').

keyTakeaways: Small files: os.ReadFile / os.WriteFile read or write the whole thing in one call. Large files: os.Open / os.Create and stream with bufio.
Always check the error from open/read/write, and defer f.Close() immediately after a successful open — close within the loop iteration to avoid descriptor leaks.
bufio.Writer buffers in memory; you must Flush (closing the file does not), and declaring defer w.Flush() after defer f.Close() makes Flush run first.
bufio.Scanner streams lines with constant memory; Scan() returns false on EOF or error, so always check scanner.Err(), and detect missing files with errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist).
